title: Road Work Zones: Don't Get Backed Over
summary: An engineering technician pushing a wheelbarrow of concrete was killed by a cement mixer backing out of a road job. He heard the alarm and tried to hurry away. Workers on foot and drivers must plan, communicate, and stay out of each other's paths.
talking_points: The technician took a concrete sample from one mixer and walked past the back of another mixer to reach his truck. The second driver had finished washing out, started backing out, and did not see him. Back-up alarms were sounding, but he was struck anyway.
Use an Internal Traffic Control Plan (ITCP) for each road work zone. It shows where and how vehicles and people on foot interact, and it should be updated as the site changes.
Where possible, drivers should drive out forward instead of backing out. Use alternate routes if they are available.
Park and work where you will not be in the path of exiting vehicles. Plan your walking route and your parking spot before you start.
Workers on foot and drivers must communicate by radio, hand signals, or eye contact. Review the agreed signals before each shift.
Before backing, the driver should walk around the vehicle, then use a trained spotter. Window down, radio off, no phone, foot on the brake. If you lose sight of the spotter, stop.

Spotters stand alone, with no phone and no crowd. They must see the driver's face in the mirror, use both hands with big motions, watch for pinch points, keep an escape route, and never turn their back on traffic.
Wear a reflective vest that is visible from all sides when you are exposed to moving equipment.

Ask about warning devices: hard-hat mirrors, parabolic mirrors, ultrasonic back-up sensors, and rear cameras. A back-up alarm alone may not be enough, especially when more than one machine is backing up.
site_hazards_to_check: Vehicles backing out of tight spaces with no spotter
Several trucks with back-up alarms sounding at the same time
Workers on foot carrying loads through equipment travel paths
Parking spots or work positions in the exit flow of trucks
discussion_questions: Where do vehicles and people on foot cross paths on this site?
What hand signals will drivers, spotters, and walkers use today?
Where will you park and walk so you are out of vehicle paths?
